Gray cushions lined the floor of the modest Downtown space, and the scent of incense lingered faintly in the air. "I've recently joined the congregation at Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha," Wallen said, "and I have to say, it's been a really positive experience for me. I feel like it's helped me to cultivate a sense of calm and clarity in my life, which is really important to me, especially with my busy schedule as a Corporate Accountant."

The Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha, founded in 2007, maintains its Downtown storefront as a space where residents can practice without agenda or expectation. Tao Lee, who helps coordinate the space, observed that such openings matter precisely when they're not compelled by crisis. "To be honest, I haven't really thought about the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha that much," Lee said, "but I do know that our neighborhood has a strong sense of community, and it's great to see places like the Telegraph Presbyterian Fellowship opening their doors for support."

This week saw faith communities across Oakland's Downtown neighborhood responding to the quiet need for gathering spaces that do not make demands. At the Telegraph Presbyterian Fellowship, just blocks away, chairs were arranged in concentric circles for evening discussions. Eunice Marston of Telegraph Presbyterian noted the shared purpose among Downtown's spiritual centers. "I haven't had any direct involvement with the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha," she said, "but as a faith leader in Downtown, I appreciate the various initiatives and organizations that bring people together and foster a sense of community."

Elliot Graye gave us something quieter this week — folding chairs at the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha, gray cushions on the floor, incense faint in the air. Cameron Wallen found something there that his schedule as a corporate accountant usually crowds out. Eunice Marston of Telegraph Presbyterian noted that Downtown's faith spaces share a purpose without necessarily sharing an address. Tao Lee's observation — that openings matter precisely when they're not compelled by crisis — is the kind of sentence I want to keep. The fog week, the illness in Chinatown, the playoff electricity: a city under pressure needs places that simply stay open without requiring anything.

In these ordinary weeks when no one is counting chairs, the practice continues. The A's, of course, broke through the fog in the way only playoff baseball can. Anthony Raines put us in the visiting clubhouse in New York where John Ellis sat with a towel over his shoulders after nine innings, four hits, zero earned runs, nine strikeouts. The A's closed the ALDS with a 4-0 win, and Ellis was not modest about what it meant: "We're here to win, and that performance was a statement." Eric Taveras, whose fourth-inning home run was the offensive signature of the night, told Raines that when your pitcher brings that kind of fire, the rest of the roster has no choice but to match it. Back in Fruitvale, Rick Walker and Rafael Pilgrim heard it on the radio and said the same thing independently — this team might have the pitching depth to go somewhere real. The question Raines left open is whether Ellis was a harbinger or an outlier. The ALCS will answer it, and I expect that answer to reverberate through every neighborhood in this city.

Taveras’ home run, his second of the series, was a solo shot in the fourth inning, part of a night where he went one-for-four with one RBI. It wasn’t a barrage of offense, but it didn’t need to be. Ellis’ performance rendered every run a luxury, not a necessity. Back in Oakland, the buzz was palpable. Rick Walker, tuning in from Fruitvale, caught the game on the radio. "I heard about John Ellis' shutout on the radio this morning—what a performance!" he said. "It’s got me thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to make a serious playoff run this year." Rafael Pilgrim echoed the sentiment: "I heard about John Ellis' shutout—nine innings, no runs. It’s got people here in Fruitvale buzzing, thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to go deep in the playoffs."

The Oaks came up twice too, and in ways that don't quite match. Talia Finch went to West Oakland and found Elio Perez and Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark all saying, with genuine warmth, that the team is reaching toward the community and that it matters. Then Simon Leary spent his week with the A's record — 127-35, a machine more than a team by now — and asked the harder question: at what point does the architecture become the story, rather than the people passing through? Martin Richards, a veteran who knows something about being moved across positions and cities, told Simon that value shifts sometimes overnight. Ollie Campbell, who doesn't even follow sports closely, noticed people talking about how the A's keep winning no matter who's holding the beams. The Oaks engagement Talia documented and the A's apparatus Simon examined are two different models of what a sports franchise can be in this city. One is still trying to be recognized by its neighborhood. The other has achieved something so structural it barely needs anyone's recognition.

Outside, the A’s were winning again. They always were. 127-35, another number in a season of numbers. What does it mean when a machine—and make no mistake, that’s what this is now, not a team but an apparatus—keeps running no matter which gears are swapped out? How does a structure like that bear its own weight? Richards, who has no answers because no one does, only the numbers, squinted at the light through the blinds. “It’s not just about adapting—it’s about understanding that your value shifts, sometimes overnight.”

The question now is whether Ellis’ performance is a harbinger of things to come or a statistical outlier. His nine strikeouts against zero walks suggest command, and the four hits allowed—all singles—indicate he kept the Yankees’ power in check. But postseason baseball is a game of small samples, and one dominant outing doesn’t guarantee a repeat. The ALCS will test whether Ellis has turned a corner or simply authored a singular masterpiece. For now, the A’s will ride the momentum. Ellis set the tone, Taveras provided just enough offense, and the team heads to the ALCS with confidence. But whether this is the start of a deeper run or a fleeting peak remains to be seen. The board speaks clearly for this game, but the ledger for the series is still unwritten.

Meanwhile, Irene Fay, a barista from a nearby coffee shop, sat at the end of the bar, looking a bit out of place. "I feel like community engagement with the Oaks team is something I've heard about, but I don't really know much about it. As a barista, I mostly just focus on my job and don't really get involved in that kind of thing," she said, looking around the bar with a curious expression. Darius Clark, a bakery worker and regular at the bar, overheard our conversation and added, "I feel like the community is pretty supportive of the Oaks team, I see people around here talking about them and it seems like they're trying to engage with us more."

The Oakland Oaks don't yet have a game on their record — preseason zero and zero — but Talia Finch and Selena Grant both found the same energy building in Downtown, the same strangers gathered around bar televisions, the same residents using the word "buzz." Head Coach Wilson Shepard told Finch the city is going to be caught off guard. Adash Stanley, the Oaks' point guard, described the whole city waking up with the team. I'll be honest: I've heard opening-season optimism before, and it doesn't always survive contact with a real schedule. What I'm watching is whether the Oaks can hold community attention in the same week the A's are deep in an ALCS. Oakland is not a city that typically has to divide its sports loyalty in October. This is new territory, and the neighborhoods will feel the split.

I walked further down Broadway, taking in the sights and sounds of the bustling neighborhood. The smell of freshly brewed coffee wafted through the air, mingling with the chatter of pedestrians. As I turned a corner, I stumbled upon a small, unnamed bar, its doors open to the street. Inside, a group of strangers were gathered around the TV, watching a replay of the Oaks' preseason game. One of them, a young man with a fervent glint in his eye, turned to me and said, "I've felt the excitement building around the Oaks, it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. There's a buzz in the air, and I think people are really looking forward to seeing what they can do this season." I later found out that he was echoing the sentiments of Adash Stanley, the Oaks' point guard, who had said, "I've felt the excitement building around the Oaks, it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. There's a buzz in the air, and I think people are really looking forward to seeing what they can do this season."

As the sun began to set, casting a warm glow over the city, I found myself back at the corner store, sipping on a coffee and reflecting on the day's conversations. The Oaks may still be an unknown quantity, but one thing is certain – the people of Downtown are hungry for success, and they're eager to see what the team can do. ============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Breath Before the Step Lonzo Jailon's fingers hover over the lake markers, tentative in the fog. His usual morning routine—checking the water levels along Lake Merritt's edge—has slowed to a methodical shuffle. The numbered posts he relies on blur into the gray, forcing him to pause, squint, double-check. "That fog rolls in and suddenly the whole lake feels like it's holding its breath," Jailon says, tucking his clipboard under his arm to rub warmth back into his hands. His role as a sea level monitor means trusting measurements, but three straight days of rain followed by this thick marine layer have left even the gulls quiet. "Been keeping to myself more than usual, just... waiting for some sunlight to punch through."

"Tomas? Yeah, he's got this energy about him—like he's always working on something bigger, even when he's just plating up orders," says Le during a rare lull, wiping her knife down. "You can tell he's listening, not just waiting for his turn to speak." Hill offers a different take between loading sheet trays into the washer: "Man keeps his head down on the line, does his job. I hear the podcast chatter sometimes when we're breaking down stations, but Harborline's not the kind of place where you bring that energy to work. We're all just trying to get through the rush."

"Man, juggling the podcast and the line cook gig at Harborline? It's all about rhythm, you know?" Renteria says, checking the doneness of three medium-rare orders with a press of his tongs. "At the grill, it's fire and timing, making sure every plate's right. Then with the mic, it's about catching that same energy but with voices and stories instead of food." Around him, the Harborline line cooks navigate the tight kitchen space—Quynh Le layering roasted vegetables with precision, Jalen Hill silently refilling the fry station as the ticket printer spits another wave of orders.

That question brushes directly against what Jax Caldera found Downtown, and what Luis Navarro found when he talked to servers in two different neighborhoods about the same civic feeling. Jax stood on those eight or nine downtown blocks where retail vitality fell nearly three points, housing pressure is now worse than eighteen of the city's twenty-two neighborhoods, and the sentiment reading has dropped to 0.41 — above the city median, so nobody gets to call it the worst, but moving in the wrong direction with nothing waiting on the other side to catch it. Eunice Marston, who watches her congregation move past SpeedyBurger every week, said she hasn't seen any significant initiatives to address the concerns. Merkin Jumper, a caseworker who notices things professionally, used the word wish. Not expect. Not demand. Wish.

Wish. That's the word doing the work. Not waiting on. Not was told. Wish — like a birthday candle, not a budget line. Here's what the record actually says, because Jumper's gut and the numbers agree for once: Downtown's sentiment reading dropped four-tenths of a point and now sits at 0.41 — eighth out of twenty-two neighborhoods, technically above the city's own median of 0.36, so don't let anybody tell you this is the worst block in town. It isn't. But retail vitality fell nearly three full points to 9.55, and housing pressure jumped a full point to 3, worse than eighteen of twenty-two neighborhoods in this city. Three metrics, three directions, all bad, all landing on the same eight or nine downtown blocks in the same stretch. And when I went looking for the initiative, the task force, the office, the anything with a name on it that's supposed to be sitting on this fire — there's nothing. No matching program. No mitigator. Nobody's desk.
